maths.problem: Malar's purse has four coins: ₹5, ₹2, ₹2 and ₹1. How much money is in the purse?
maths.explain: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 5, then 7, then 9, then 10. So the purse holds ₹10.
maths.context: In the Two Plates Test you found how much a plate of coins was worth. Here you do it by counting on, without chana.
maths.why_maths: Counting on from the biggest coin is adding. It is how a shopkeeper counts your money in a few seconds.

maths.problem: Kavya has three ₹2 coins. Arjun has five ₹1 coins. A pencil costs ₹6. Who can buy the pencil?
maths.explain: Kavya has 2, 4, 6: that is ₹6, the same as the price. Arjun has ₹5, which is one less than 6. So only Kavya has enough, though she has fewer coins.
maths.context: In the Two Plates Test, the plate with fewer coins sometimes bought more. Here two children have different coins and one price to pay.
maths.why_maths: To know who has enough, you compare each amount with the price. Comparing numbers answers the question 'can I buy it?'.

maths.problem: Find three different ways to pay ₹6 with ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins.
maths.explain: Each way must add up to 6. There are five ways in all. The other two are 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 and six ₹1 coins.
maths.context: In Ten Rupees, Many Ways you paid ₹10 with different coins. Here you do the same for ₹6.
maths.why_maths: Breaking a number into parts in different ways lets you pay with whatever coins you happen to have.

maths.problem: You have ₹20. A balloon costs ₹2, a chikki costs ₹8 and a notebook costs ₹15. Which two things can you NOT buy together?
maths.explain: Add each pair. Balloon and chikki: 2 + 8 = 10. Balloon and notebook: 2 + 15 = 17. Chikki and notebook: 8 + 15 = 23. Only 23 is more than 20.
maths.context: In Our Home Shop you had ₹20 and chose what to buy. Here is the same kind of choice with three price tags.
maths.why_maths: Adding the prices before you pay tells you whether your money will be enough. This is the question 'how much can we spend?'.

maths.problem: This goes past Class 1. A machine gives only ₹2 coins. Which of these prices can you pay exactly: ₹6, ₹7 or ₹8?
maths.explain: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. You say 6 and 8, but you jump over 7. To pay ₹7 you would need a ₹1 coin as well. This is one reason we have ₹1 coins.
maths.context: In the fewest coins puzzle you saw that the kinds of coin we have decide how easy each price is to pay. Here there is only one kind.
maths.why_maths: Counting in twos shows a pattern: every second number is missed. The pattern tells you which prices cannot be paid.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Plates Test, one ₹10 coin bought more chana than eight ₹1 coins. The ₹10 coin is not ten times as big or as heavy. It is worth ten because everyone agrees that it is. So the worth of a coin is not inside the coin. It is a promise that people keep with each other.
deep_truth.habit: We think a coin is worth ten by itself, the way a mango is sweet by itself. But a coin is worth ten only while people agree to take it for ten.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Plates Test, one coin beat eight coins. And in 2016 the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes stopped being money in one night, though the paper had not changed.

three.who_am_i: You are one of the people who make money work. Each time you take a coin and trust it, you keep the promise going.
three.what_is_life: Every living being gives and takes. A bee takes nectar and carries pollen for the flower. People made coins to keep count of their giving and taking.
three.what_is_this_world: A ₹5 banana needed the sun, the rain, the soil, a banana plant and a farmer. The ₹5 pays only the people. The sun and the rain ask for nothing.

roots.thread: Money starts from one rupee. Two rupees is one and one more. A ₹10 coin is ten ones made into a single coin. So one coin can hold many, and many coins can be swapped for one. The one and the many are the same amount.

teachings.teaching: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,300 years ago, says that money exists by agreement and not by nature. He says people have the power to change it, or to make it useless.
teachings.link: This is what the Two Plates Test and the old ₹500 notes both show. The worth is in what people agree, not in the metal or the paper.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching, an old Chinese book, says: the one who knows they have enough is rich.
teachings.link: In this lesson you asked 'Do I have enough?' and answered it by counting. Enough is not the biggest heap. It is the amount that meets the need.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says: this world is not for those who have no wealth, and the other world is not for those who have no kindness.
teachings.link: Money buys what a shop sells, and a family needs it. The Kural puts kindness beside it as the other thing a person needs, and no coin can buy that.

science.text: On 8 November 2016, the government of India announced that the ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes of that time would stop being money at midnight. The paper stayed the same. Only the agreement changed.
What makes money worth something? Some say trust between people. Some say the government's rule. Some say it must stand for something useful, like gold. People who study money still argue about it.

other_view.who: Many people through history, and a few thinkers about money today
other_view.view: They say good money must be worth something by itself. Old rupee coins were made of silver, and the silver could be melted and sold. A paper note is only a promise, and a promise can be broken. Silver and gold stay worth something even when people stop trusting each other.

how_we_found_out.context: How did money begin? This card tells how one old story about it was checked, and found to have no proof.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people who wrote about money told one story. Long ago, they said, nobody had money, and everyone swapped things: a pot for a fish, a goat for a sack of rice. Swapping was hard, so people invented coins. A Scottish thinker, Adam Smith, wrote this in a famous book in 1776. But nobody had checked. In 1985 Caroline Humphrey, who studies how people live at the University of Cambridge, read the reports from villages all over the world. She wrote that no one had ever described a people who lived by swapping alone. In small villages, people mostly gave things to their neighbours and remembered who owed what. So keeping count of who owes whom may be older than coins. The first coins we know of in India are small pieces of silver with marks stamped on them, made about 2,500 years ago. The word rupee comes from the rupiya, a silver coin made by the ruler Sher Shah Suri in the 1540s.
how_we_found_out.who: Caroline Humphrey, who checked a story told by Adam Smith and many others
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Before money, everyone lived by swapping things. In 1985 Caroline Humphrey showed that nobody had ever found a people who lived that way.
